replacements.148: Selecting CB-FL-S established the strongest RAW process baseline for regional grapevine phenology, but substantial predictable error remained. The additional DEM gain within hybrids was only 0.12 d. Thus, process selection and subsequent correction address related prediction problems, and their individual gains cannot be assumed to add together.
replacements.150: The controlled advantages of linear forcing and sequential interaction were larger than the effect of chilling-response shape. This supports prioritizing forcing response and the timing of chilling–forcing interaction when choosing among the tested formulations. The small sequential–parallel difference at veraison also shows that an overall ranking can obscure stage dependence. Limited benefits of greater complexity have previously been reported for grapevine models (Fila et al., 2014), whereas nonlinear responses have improved predictions under other experimental and climatic conditions (Sadras and Moran, 2013; Thomas et al., 2026). Such differences are compatible with dependence on temperature range, cultivar composition and the particular response function.
replacements.151: These rankings apply to fixed cardinal temperatures and seasonal origins with separately fitted accumulation thresholds. Beta-forcing structures failed to meet all early-stage calibration bias targets, so their poorer performance also reflects the fit achieved under the constrained objective. The sequential advantage is likewise conditional on the implemented parallel competence function and its minimum value of 0.2. Equal event-date accuracy need not imply equivalent physiological representations (Chuine and Régnière, 2017). Controlled temperature experiments and independent dormancy observations would help determine whether alternative parameterizations preserve these rankings.
replacements.152: Veraison and maturity/harvest remained harder to predict, although their different site and observation populations prevent attribution to development alone. Later simulated dates inherit preceding-stage timing, which changes the weather encountered during subsequent accumulation; later conditions can amplify or compensate for earlier errors. Chilling acts directly only before budburst in this implementation, so its apparent maturity benefit can arise through this sequence. Observed differences in interval sensitivity and cultivar thermal requirements support these dependencies (Cameron et al., 2022; Parker et al., 2013). Shared thresholds average over that diversity. BBCH89 additionally combines fruit development with harvest decisions, unlike a specified sugar-ripeness target (Parker et al., 2020). Relationships between harvest timing, temperature and moisture identify plausible missing information, but do not explain individual residuals in this collection (Cook and Wolkovich, 2016).
replacements.157: 4.2 When elevation correction improves phenology prediction
replacements.158: DEM correction remains relevant because it improved every process structure and reduced their average MAE by 8.4%. Its value is clearest when process models are used without residual learning; the small hybrid increment answers a different question. Improvement at only 61–66% of sites across stages indicates that a uniform elevation adjustment addresses part of temperature representativeness. Vineyard measurements show spatial and canopy-related variation in meteorological conditions (Matese et al., 2014), while seasonal lapse rates and inversions can depart from a constant adjustment (Rolland, 2003). Consequently, elevation information alone cannot capture the full local temperature environment.
replacements.159: Sites below the weather-grid elevation benefited more than those above it. Under the specified lapse rate, the former receive warmer temperatures and the latter cooler temperatures. The observed asymmetry therefore concerns the direction of fitted temperature-input changes, rather than a general rule that larger mismatch requires greater correction. Temperature shifts can influence chilling, forcing and subsequent accumulation differently, and terrain classes also differ in cultivar, country and environmental composition. These explanations remain hypotheses. Likewise, local terrain variability and regional relief describe surrounding heterogeneity rather than the elevation offset at an individual site, explaining why they are not interchangeable guides to correction benefit.
replacements.160: The average gain persisted under alternative weighting and exclusion sensitivities, supporting its relevance within the sampled population. However, separate threshold recalibration is part of the treatment contrast: lower phenological error cannot establish that corrected daily temperatures are closer to observations. Independent site temperatures are needed to assess that claim and to test seasonally varying lapse rates. For hybrid applications, the near-zero average increment and local reversals support evaluating DEM correction against final stage-specific error rather than including it automatically. Its limited additional value here does not imply that finer-scale temperature information is unnecessary in other environments.
replacements.161: 4.3 Residual learning and its overlap with temperature correction
replacements.162: Residual learning improved all forty model–stage combinations, demonstrating that information useful for date prediction remained beyond shared process thresholds. The design combines stage-specific observed-minus-process residuals with process-state and environmental predictors, using TabM as the regression architecture (Gorishniy et al., 2025). Its contribution lies in this process-guided residual formulation, rather than a new base neural architecture. Process-predicted dates and phase durations summarize simulated seasonal progress and can distinguish situations in which the process model is systematically early or late. Temperature summaries over the preceding 7, 30 and 90 days describe recent conditions beyond the accumulated thermal requirement. Day length and terrain provide seasonal and spatial context that may help distinguish residual patterns under otherwise similar process states. This combination follows the broader rationale for integrating process understanding with flexible statistical prediction (Reichstein et al., 2019).
replacements.163: Residual targets come from observations excluded from their corresponding process fit, with grouped nested fitting also protecting neural validation from process-label reuse. This links learning to errors outside the fitted observations rather than merely reproducing apparent calibration residuals. Nevertheless, the predictive contribution of each feature group remains unresolved. Process-state, weather and terrain information can covary with cultivar composition, management and observation practice. Lower test MAE establishes their joint predictive usefulness under the evaluation design, without identifying a forcing, physiological or management mechanism. Feature-removal comparisons and independent temperature observations would be needed to distinguish these explanations. No such ablation result is implied by the aggregate gains.
replacements.164: Residual correction compressed the process-model MAE range from 11.27–14.61 to 8.30–8.75 d on the common population. This reduced sensitivity to process structure, but did not make gain alone a suitable selection criterion: the gain contains baseline error arithmetically, and the model with the largest correction did not have the lowest final MAE. The different process and hybrid winners also show why both correction approaches required evaluation across all ten structures. Date correction leaves thermal attainment unchanged, so it improves event-time estimates without repairing a process model's failure to reach a developmental requirement.
replacements.165: DEM benefit declined from 1.06 d for process models to 0.12 d for hybrids, a paired decrease of 0.94 d; relative benefits similarly declined from 8.4% to 1.4%. This is consistent with overlap in the errors addressed: terrain and weather predictors may help residual learners account for repeatable discrepancies associated with temperature representativeness. Other remaining errors may concern cultivar, management or endpoint heterogeneity beyond a lapse-rate adjustment. These interpretations are not identified mechanisms, because both process thresholds and residual learners were refitted under each temperature input. The evidence establishes limited additional average DEM value within the sampled domain, not reconstruction of local temperature by the learner or equivalence of RAW and DEM hybrids.
replacements.168: The grouped holdout evaluates retrospective estimation at withheld sites within represented temperature regimes. Keeping shared weather cells and overlapping locations together reduces dependence, consistent with matching validation to the prediction setting (Roberts et al., 2017), but nearby groups can retain similar environments and management. Environmental-zone contrasts therefore describe heterogeneity within the primary holdout rather than independent regional transfer. Their changing error rankings after correction reinforce the importance of final stage-specific performance, while sparse flowering support in the coldest zone and limited maturity observations elsewhere prevent broad climatic conclusions.
replacements.169: Geographic and endpoint imbalance further constrain interpretation. Germany contributes nearly three quarters of the observations, whereas France supplies almost all maturity/harvest records. Equal-site weighting limits dominance by long records but does not balance countries or supply missing country–stage combinations. Incomplete cultivar and plant identities, repeated dates and mixed harvest endpoints limit separation of biological variation from management and observation effects. The 4 November assignment also makes late-season scores a measure under a common administrative convention; raw attainment and assignment frequencies remain necessary alongside MAE. Pointwise intervals concern individual contrasts without adjustment for multiple comparisons.
replacements.170: Screening and calibration procedures were revised after preliminary model results became available. Final process fitting and neural tuning exclude test labels, but the full development process lacks a prospectively untouched evaluation cohort. Screening and weather eligibility may also exclude genuine extremes, and comparisons with historical runs cannot isolate a cleaning effect because eligibility and calibration changed together. Independent observations with prespecified screening, consistent endpoints and cultivar identities are therefore priorities, alongside withheld-region and unusually warm-season tests of ranking stability.
replacements.171: Predictions use realized weather through process-predicted dates. Their retrospective accuracy does not establish performance at an advance forecast issue date, which requires evaluation using only information available at issuance. Similarly, corrected dates are external adjustments to the simulated thermal state; coupling them to canopy, water-demand or crop-protection models requires an explicit, separately tested rule. More accurate phenological dates may support vineyard decisions, but effects on frost damage, fruit composition, yield or management outcomes remain unevaluated.
replacements.181: Regional grapevine phenology was evaluated through comparison of ten process structures and further improvement with terrain-based temperature correction and a process-guided residual model, using observations from 3,169 sites in 11 countries. CB-FL-S achieved the lowest RAW process MAE, 11.31 d on its model-specific finite-scoring population and 11.27 d on the common paired population. Across all ten structures, DEM correction reduced process MAE by 1.06 d, while RAW residual learning reduced it by 4.10 d and narrowed final hybrid MAE to 8.30–8.75 d.
replacements.182: DEM correction added only 0.12 d to average hybrid accuracy, with an interval spanning zero. Thus, gains from temperature correction and residual learning were not additive. Model selection requires final stage-specific error and process attainment alongside correction magnitude. These results support structure selection followed by joint evaluation of correction options for retrospective estimation within the sampled environments; independent validation is needed to establish regional transfer and operational forecasting performance.
